newsitem.title: ROMANIA: New Ukraine treaty stirs old passions in Romania.
newsitem.headline: New Ukraine treaty stirs old passions in Romania.

text.p: Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin on Wednesday defended a post-communist treaty with nearby Ukraine that has disturbed many in Romania.

Reformist President Emil Constantinescu convened political leaders at his Cotroceni palace, saying he wanted public debate on the document which he is expected to formally sign with Ukrainian counterpart Leonid Kuchma.

The treaty, three years in the making, may improve Bucharest's chances of gaining early NATO membership. Both sides recognise existing borders and pledge themselves to raise no territorial claims against each other.
"This is the best time to conclude the treaty with Ukraine," Severin told a show aired by a local broadcaster.
"Nobody has put pressure on us to conclude it," he said of the treaty he initialled with his Ukrainian opposite number Hennady Udovenko in Kiev last Saturday.
Severin rejected Romanian nationalists' accusations that he had signed away heartlands which Romania lost to Moscow under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact and are now part of modern Ukraine.

"I know that Romania is grieving over the loss of its heartlands to the Soviet Union in 1940," he said. "But in the present circumstances, we can be reunited with our Romanian kin in Ukraine only within an integrated Europe."
Bucharest dropped its previous insistence that Kiev atone for Romania's losses in the Ribbentrop-Molotov pact, which carved up Eastern Europe between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
"The Ukrainians had some fears which we understood," Severin said. "Ukraine fears it could face territorial claims from all its neighbours. Its least problems are with Romania."

The issue of atonement for Romania's territorial losses and the displacement of its population under the 1939 pact remains the main stumbling bloc to concluding similar treaties with the Russian Federation and ex-Soviet Moldova.
"We don't have anything to reproach to Ukraine over that pact, but we have things to reproach to Russia, the main successor to the former Soviet Union," Severin said.
Romania won praise from the West for signing a treaty with Hungary last year ending old rifts over borders and minorities with its Central European neighbour.

Some Western leaders have said a similar deal with Kiev could boost Bucharest's chances of gaining early admission to NATO, along with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, when the Alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a July summit in Madrid.

On Wednesday the Romanian foreign ministry said remaining differences with Ukraine over delineating borders in the Black Sea, which both sides believe is rich in natural gas and oil, would be resolved as part of a separate treaty.

Ministry spokeswoman Gilda Lazar said the two sides had agreed on "a two-year moratorium on works or on conducting joint drills" on the sea shelf at dispute, which experts say extends over some 7,000 square km (4,000 square miles).
